newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Belgian justice learns from paedophile case bungle.
newsitem.headline: Belgian justice learns from paedophile case bungle.

text.p: Belgium's justice minister pledged on Wednesday to make investigations into organised crime more efficient and chase up slow-moving cases after accusations of police bungling in a child sex and murder scandal.
"The events of recent weeks have shown there is a problem concerning...the contacts between the police, the magistrature and the state prosecution," Justice Minister Stefaan De Clerck told reporters.
Announcing he was drawing up a directive to improve these links, he told a news conference: "You have to know who is doing what, and when."
De Clerck was speaking after a three-day policy meeting with Belgium's five attorney generals on judicial reform.

Public confidence in the Belgian legal system was shaken when convicted child rapist Marc Dutroux, who had been released from a 13-year jail sentence ten years early, on August 17 led police to the bodies of two eight year olds in his garden.

Julie Lejeune and Melissa Russo had vanished in June 1995. The investigation into their disappearence has since been revealed to be a catalogue of bungling, incompetence and rivalry between different police forces and the judiciary.
It has even prompted speculation about possible police complicity, which could have allowed Dutroux to remain undetected for so long despite being known to the authorities.

The remains of two teenage girls, missing for a year, were found at another of Dutroux's properties. Two more were rescued alive, but sexually abused, from a home-made dungeon in another of his houses around Charleroi, southern Belgium.
Altogether 13 people have been arrested in the paedophile, kidnapping and murder case and in a related car theft ring investigation.
De Clerck said the attorney generals had also been told to look at ways to speed up slow-moving investigations.
"We need to see how we can speed up the advancement of these dossiers," he said, adding that cases which dragged on for more than six months would come special focus.
De Clerck said another of his priorities was the problem of child pornography on the Internet. He planned to set up a special police team to fight the problem.
